1000318.etyen:

Standard Bokmål på (“on, at”) ultimately contains the same preposition, having developed from Old Norse upp á (“up on”).

1000830.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Etnardalr, from the genitive Etnar of the old river name Etn, followed by dalr (“valley”), literally “valley of the Etna”. The modern form is analysable as Etna + dal (“valley”); when the river name occurs as the first element of the compound, its final -a is traditionally dropped, giving unlinked Etne-.
The deeper origin of the river name is uncertain; it has been connected with Old Norse etja (“to urge, drive forward”) or eta (“to eat”).

1001086.etyen:
Either ultimately from Biblical Hebrew חַנָּה (“grace, favour”), from the root חָנַן (“to be gracious”), or a short form of Johanna. The latter origin has historically been the more important in Norway. Johanna continues Latin Iohanna, the feminine form of Iohannes, from Ancient Greek Ἰωάννης (Iōánnēs), ultimately from Biblical Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (“Yahweh is gracious”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Hanna, Danish Hanna, Swedish Hanna, Icelandic Hanna and English Hannah.
